We formally announced Mirendil less than 4 months ago. Today, I'm excited to share an important milestone for:

Pretraining at scale without a pretraining team.

Mirendil's mission is to solve Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) and use it to democratize frontier AI development, ultimately accelerating science and technology. At Mirendil, when we think about RSI, we think holistically about the company as an intelligent entity that self-improves toward its goal. From that perspective, the most powerful notion of acceleration is reducing the time and resources (number of human experts, compute, and other costs) needed to achieve ambitious goals.

Given that pretraining is perhaps the most important yet most challenging part of frontier AI development, we decided to run an ambitious controlled experiment: Starting fully from scratch, can we significantly reduce the time, number of human experts, and compute resources needed to go all the way to successfully pretraining a strong coding model at scale?

Mirendil-Base is the result of this experiment. Our first pretrained model was built by one researcher in 3.5 months, with less than $10M in compute. This includes all the research and small-scale experiments it took to get there, as well as the final training run.

The recipe holds up as the models get bigger. For reference, Mirendil-Base is in the 100B-500B parameter range, Mirendil-Base-Large in the 500B-2T range, and Mirendil-Base-XL in the 2T-10T range.

We're beginning to see a world where a single researcher, empowered by AI, can take on work that once required an entire research organization. As these systems improve, the bottleneck shifts from the size of a team to the ambition and judgment of the people directing them. This has profound implications for who gets to build AI and, ultimately, who gets to push the frontiers of science and technology forward.

We’ll share independent evaluations, post-training benchmarks and API-access sooner than you think so stay tuned!

I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. Great piece of “The Prestige” lore is that Nolan says the only person to ever turn him down for an acting role was David Bowie (his idol).

Nolan begged for a meeting and finally convinced Bowie by rewriting the scene when he shows up as Nikola Tesla: 

“The only ‘no’ I would cop to is David Bowie for ‘The Prestige.’ He was my great idol and everything, and I thought he'd be perfect to play Nikola Tesla.

We sent him the script and everything. He said ‘no’. 

It was first time really ever, I went back and said, ‘Can I just go and meet him? Can I try and convince him in the room?’

They agreed, and I hastily wrote him a better speech for his first appearance, turned up with a new script, and…basically begged and got him to do it. So I turned the ‘no’ into a ‘yes.’”

quoted.text:
One of the great coincidences in finance:

In 1952 Harry Markowitz published "Portfolio Selection." It became the foundation of modern asset management. The idea is that you optimize a diversified basket of assets along an efficient frontier by claiming to know what the currently “efficient” part of the frontier is (even though no one actually knows which assets will perform most efficiently in the future). 

That same year a British actuary named Frank Redington published "Review of the Principles of Life-Office Valuations." It showed how institutions could immunize their liabilities by matching them with assets across time. It became the foundation of institutional asset-liability matching. Almost nobody outside of insurance and banking knows it.

The interesting thing is institutions adopted Redington because matching assets to liabilities is just the sensible way to manage cash flows. Meanwhile the industry sold Markowitz to retail investors….
